newsitem.title: CYPRUS: FEATURE - Scarred Rwandan orphan given new life in Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Scarred Rwandan orphan given new life in Cyprus.

text.p: The young girl cheerfully skipping up the stairs bears little resemblance to the scarred, frightened child who arrived in Cyprus from Rwanda just six months ago.
The scars are still there under the frilly white collar of her floral print dress but they have been smoothed out by a plastic surgeon's knife.
Thirteen-year-old Julienne Uwase was flown to Cyprus last October so disfigured by severe burns on the upper part of her body that she could hardly raise her arms or lift her chin.
Fate had dealt her two cruel blows in quick succession.
First her parents were killed before her eyes during the genocide that ravaged her African homeland in 1994.
Barely a month later, when she had been moved into an orphanage, her clothes caught fire from an oil lamp.
Her future looked bleak. As the burns healed, the scar tissue on her upper arms and chest stuck together. And her chin was virtually stuck to her neck. She had little mobility from the waist up.
Now she has been given a new lease of life, thanks to the missionary zeal of a Danish mother and daughter and the caring spirit of the people of this Mediterranean island.

Doctors did plastic surgery for free in two major operations in the capital Nicosia and local residents opened their homes and their hearts to Julienne as she recuperated, helped by her Rwandan nurse Josephine Kamagaju.
GOING HOME WITH NEW CLOTHES AND TOYS
The first stage of her treatment is now finished and they leave Cyprus on Sunday to return to Rwanda, Julienne loaded down with toys and new clothes given by wellwishers.
She will need more surgery as her body develops and is due to come back in three years for further operations.
She giggles and nods shyly when asked if she speaks Greek, then willingly obliges with three or four phrases picked up from Cypriot nursing staff.
"It is sad to leave," Julienne says in halting English. "But I miss my family."
What's left of her family is four sisters and two brothers. She will rejoin them in the orphanage in her home town of Biumba.
Kamagaju too lost her parents in the mass slaughter by Hutu extremists in 1994, also two brothers, three sisters and the man she was going to marry.
Now she and Julienne have found a new parent in Ingelis Jensen, 52, a Danish social worker with the Seventh Day Adventist Church who has been living in Cyprus for the past seven years.
"She's our mum," says Kamagaju, giving Jensen a hug.
"We have a parent-child relationship," explains Jensen, sitting between the two at her apartment in Nicosia.
"They are part of our family now. After Sunday we will have to write a lot more letters," she says with a sorrowful smile.
Jensen first heard about Julienne's plight from her daughter Nicola, a missionary who visited the orphanage.
MISSIONARY TURNS TO CYPRUS FOR HELP
Initial attempts to send the child to Britain for surgery fell through. So the Jensens turned closer to home and found the Cypriots more than willing to help.
The national airline Cyprus Airways donated the tickets to bring Julienne and Kamagaju to Cyprus and the Greek-Cypriot government promptly offered to provide free medical treatment.
"The Health Ministry has been marvellous. They immediately accepted it as a charity case and Julienne was here within the month. We are very thankful to them," Jensen said.

In between operations, Julienne has been receiving schooling from Kamagaju. She has been living the life of any other carefree 13-year-old on the island -- learning how to ride a bicycle to chase after the icecream man and playing the piano.
Of the future, Julienne says solemnly: "I want to help other children ...(to) be a teacher."
Jensen adds: "She is very clever. She knows that things will be different when she goes back and that these are two different worlds."
